findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: Every cleanup batch logs at Error level: `Annotations to clean by time/count`, `cleaned annotations ...`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). Each message includes the full `ids` slice, which can hold up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands), and the `err` value, which is always nil at the fetch log sites. The final batch of every loop logs an empty result at Error too. In production this floods logs with huge false error entries on every cleanup run and can trigger error-based alerting. These look like debugging leftovers and should be removed or moved to Debug level without the ID lists.

findings.title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The ticker driving all cleanup jobs changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the PR's stated goal and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, adding database load and more chances for lock contention, which is the problem this PR is trying to reduce. It also no longer fits the 9-minute per-run timeout in `clean()`, which was sized for a 10-minute interval. This looks like a testing leftover and should be reverted.

findings.title: Bound-parameter path can exceed placeholder limits on MySQL/Postgres
findings.body: Only SQLite falls back to inlining the IDs. On MySQL and Postgres, `deleteByIDs` always binds one placeholder per ID. Both databases cap a prepared statement at 65535 parameters. If an operator sets `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that limit, every cleanup batch fails, whereas the previous subquery-based statement had no parameter limit. Consider capping or chunking the IDs per statement, or inlining the integer IDs for all dialects.

findings.title: Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs
findings.body: The loop at lines 610-612 runs `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` once per ID. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With the large batch sizes this branch exists for (e.g. 32767, as in the new test), that means heavy allocation and CPU work on every batch. Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a single byte buffer instead.
